summary:
Düzce stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been converted into documented state practice. The province's own record yields no distinct local finding, so the assessment below rests on the nationwide regime a visitor to Düzce is subject to, including at police checkpoints, in medical facilities and in document controls that apply equally in interior provinces.

Turkish law itself is not the immediate hazard. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since the 1858 Ottoman penal code, and legal gender change has been available since 1988. Turkish marriage law, however, gives same-sex relationships no recognition and provides no civil unions, domestic partnerships or joint adoption, and no comprehensive statute bans discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBT people are barred from open service in the armed forces.

The immediate hazard is a draft law. The leaked 11th Judicial Package omnibus draft, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment. The same package would sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare by imposing a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility conditions, and would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification is protecting "the family" and "public morals". The package also carries unrelated measures such as longer child sentences and online-content removal.

Enforcement has outpaced legislation. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

The passport-carrying rule compounds these risks. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Amnesty International recorded that Pride events and LGBTQ gatherings were repeatedly disallowed in 2024 and 2025, with police detaining participants. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Turkish rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

In early 2026 Turkish media reported that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex'; that provision was not included in that year's judicial reform package. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people, and is cited here as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

outOfScopeNotes:
The Düzce-specific source inventory contains no usable finding, so no claim in this record is sourced to Düzce province itself; the assessment rests entirely on the national framework and on examples drawn from Istanbul, Ankara and Kayseri. Whether Düzce police operate equivalent GBT checkpoints is unresolved and not sourced.

As of the reporting dates cited, the 11th Judicial Package remained a draft and had not been passed; its status after October 2025 is unresolved in this inventory. The separate 2026 proposal on public advocacy was reported as considered but not included in that year's judicial reform package, and its current status is unresolved.

The claim that the Yaşam case and the Poyraz death evidence a state policy of hate is the position of activists and rights groups as reported, not a judicial finding; no court ruling on either case is sourced here.

Whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation restricts access to transition care in practice, as opposed to changing record-keeping, is unresolved; the inventory reports the risk of profiling and restricted access rather than documented outcomes.
